description: 100 deep logical questions on __init__, __new__, and __del__ methods in Python OOP

questions.answer:
new A
init A

WHY: When you call A(), Python runs type.__call__: it calls A.__new__(cls) first and only if that returns an instance of A (or a subclass) does it then call A.__init__(self) on the very same object. The two hooks are invoked back-to-back, and the allocation (__new__) is always sequenced ahead of initialization (__init__).

running init
TypeError: __init__() should return None, not 'int'

WHY: The language contract for __init__ is that it merely initializes the already-allocated object and must return None. CPython enforces this in type_call: if the result of calling tp_init (__init__) is not None, it raises TypeError before propagating. The object was already created by __new__, so returning a value is useless here and simply makes the whole call fail.

new B
A

WHY: B.__new__ returns an instance of an unrelated class A, which is not an instance of B. Because type_call only invokes __init__ when the object returned by __new__ is an instance of the requested class (a subtype), B.__init__ (and A.__init__ too) are silently skipped. The variable b ends up holding a plain A object, so type(b).__name__ is 'A'.

questions.question:
Can __new__ hand state to __init__ before it runs?
```python
class A:
    def __new__(cls):
        obj = object.__new__(cls)
        obj.stamp = 'set in __new__'
        print('__new__:', obj.stamp)
        return obj
    def __init__(self):
        print('__init__:', self.stamp)

A()
```
questions.answer:
__new__: set in __new__
__init__: set in __new__

WHY: __new__ fully runs and returns the finished instance first, so any attribute it set on that instance is already present when __init__ receives it. __init__ then reads self.stamp, which was installed during allocation.

questions.question:
Classic singleton trap - predict all lines:
```python
class Singleton:
    _inst = None
    def __new__(cls, *args, **kwargs):
        if cls._inst is None:
            cls._inst = object.__new__(cls)
            print('creating fresh')
        return cls._inst
    def __init__(self, v):
        self.v = v
        print('__init__ value =', v)

a = Singleton(1)
b = Singleton(2)
print(a is b, a.v, b.v)
```
questions.answer:
creating fresh
__init__ value = 1
__init__ value = 2
True 2 2

WHY: __new__ returns the SAME cached instance on every call, but __init__ is re-invoked on that same object each time. So a and b are identical, but each construction rebinds self.v, and both see the latest value 2. A raw singelton via __new__ caching behaves like a mutable one-shot: later constructor calls silently overwrite earlier state.

questions.question:
Trace this object-pool misuse - exact order and last line:
```python
class A:
    _pool = None
    def __new__(cls, *args, **kwargs):
        if cls._pool is None:
            cls._pool = object.__new__(cls)
            print('one object allocated')
        print('__new__ returns id', id(cls._pool))
        return cls._pool
    def __init__(self, n):
        self.n = n

print('before')
x = A(10)
y = A(20)
z = A(30)
print(x is y is z, [x.n, y.n, z.n])
```
questions.answer:
before
one object allocated
__new__ returns id 139845612345600
__new__ returns id 139845612345600
__new__ returns id 139845612345600
True [30, 30, 30]

WHY: 'one object allocated' prints once because only the first call creates the instance; the ids printed are all the same (addresses vary per run). Because __init__ runs on that one shared object three times, n is overwritten each time, ending as 30 on the very same object, so all three names point to it and [30, 30, 30] is printed.

attr ok: extra
5 MyInt

WHY: int.__new__(cls, '101', 2) parses base-2 '101' into the integer 5 while still returning an instance of the subclass MyInt. A Python-level int subclass gets its own instance dict by default (no __slots__), so setting n.tag works rather than raising AttributeError. The identity of the allocation cost is that int's own slot tnew is called explicitly with cls so a MyInt, not an int, is created.

__init__ sees 'HI'
HI

WHY: str cannot be initialized and does not accept extra building work, so the only way to customize a str subclass is to craft the value inside __new__. super().__new__(cls, text.upper()) creates the instance 'HI'; every public operation of str bypasses the subclass, but __new__/__init__ are honored. __init__ receives the ORIGINAL arguments ('hi'), yet self is already the transformed 'HI' string.

__init__: (1, 2, 3)
(1, 2, 3)

WHY: tuple.__new__(cls, items) converts the iterable into the tuple (1, 2, 3) and returns a T instance, after which our __init__ runs and shows the already-converted value. The list only ever existed during the call; __init__ prints the tuple, and printing t shows the same immutable tuple.

b'h\xc3\xa9llo' héllo 6

WHY: bytes is immutable and has no reversible __init__, so the encoding happens in __new__: the str 'héllo' becomes the utf-8 bytes b'h\xc3\xa9llo' (the é occupies 2 bytes). b.decode() turns those bytes back into the original text, and len(b) counts the 6 raw bytes, not the 5 characters.

questions.question:
What happens when __new__ returns None?
```python
class A:
    def __new__(cls):
        print('__new__')
        return None
    def __init__(self):
        print('__init__ never runs')

a = A()
print(a)
```
questions.answer:
__new__
None

WHY: __new__ may legally return None, and None is not an instance of A, so __init__ is never called. The call expression A() evaluates to that very None, which is assigned to a and printed as None. No error is raised - a silently 'failed' construction.

cls is B

WHY: Although __new__ is defined on A, it is invoked as a special method of B, so Python passes B - the class being instantiated - as cls, never the defining class A. object.__new__(cls) then allocates an instance whose actual type is B; this is exactly how __new__ cooperates with inheritance.

__new__
__init__

WHY: super().__new__(cls) resolves through the MRO to object.__new__(cls), which allocates a plain A instance - a perfectly valid result. Since that result is an instance of A, the machinery immediately follows up with __init__. This is the canonical shape of a minimal, correctly overridden __new__.

B.__new__
A.__new__
B.__init__
A.__init__

WHY: allocof: B.__new__ runs, then super().__new__ walks the MRO to A.__new__ and finally object.__new__. Only after allocation completes does initialization start, top-down: B.__init__ first, then A.__init__ via super(). The two phases are not interleaved - all __new__ calls complete before any __init__ call begins, then init digs down the same chain.

A.__new__
A.__init__
B.__init__

WHY: C inherits A.__new__ (B defines none), called once with cls=C; super() from within A continues the MRO C -> A -> B -> object, reaching object.__new__. Then C's init is A.__init__, whose super() que is B.__init__, forming a linear chain even though B is only an unmixed sibling at the C level.

questions.question:
Argument unpacking in __init__ using *args and **kwargs. Predict the output:
```python
class Point:
    def __init__(self, *args, **kwargs):
        self.seen_args = args
        self.seen_kwargs = kwargs

p = Point(1, 2, 3, x=9)
print(p.seen_args, p.seen_kwargs)
```
questions.answer:
(1, 2, 3) {'x': 9}

WHY: The positional arguments land in the tuple args (1, 2, 3), and the single keyword x=9 lands in the dict kwargs as {'x': 9}. __init__ is just an ordinary method - *args/**kwargs collect whatever the constructor was given, exactly as in any other function.

new
init start
caught
del 139790045226960

WHY: __new__ completes and __init__ starts, but 'boom' aborts construction before the object is handed to the caller. Crucially, the raising __init__ frame still holds self, and the frame stays alive until the traceback is released by the except clause - so __del__ fires only AFTER 'caught', when the frame (and with it the instance) is torn down. The 'del <id>' address varies per run.

working...
caught
del sees no name attribute

WHY: The instance is fully allocated but its __dict__ is still empty when the exception fires, so the subsequent __del__ finds no 'name' attribute and prints the fallback message. The ordering (caught before del) is the same as the previous question: the failing frame keeps self alive until the traceback is dropped at the except clause.

questions.question:
Timing of __del__ under reference counting. Predict the exact output:
```python
class A:
    def __del__(self):
        print('bye', id(self))

a = A()
del a
print('main still running')
```
questions.answer:
bye 139956562517840
main still running

WHY: CPython frees the instance immediately when `del a` drops the last reference, so __del__ runs before the next statement - there is no wait for garbage collection. The interpreter continues normally afterwards, printing the main message. The id is the object address and differs between runs.

questions.question:
Circular reference: refcount alone cannot free these two objects. Predict the output:
```python
import gc

class A:
    def __init__(self, name):
        self.name = name
    def __del__(self):
        print('del', self.name)

x = A('x')
y = A('y')
x.pair = y
y.pair = x
del x, y
print('after del (refcount finds nothing)')
gc.collect()
print('after gc.collect()')
```
questions.answer:
after del (refcount finds nothing)
del x
del y
after gc.collect()

WHY: After del x, y neither reference count drops to zero because x.pair and y.pair form a cycle, so refcount-based deallocation sleeps and __del__ is not called. Calling gc.collect() breaks the cycle; the garbage collector finalizes both objects, invoking __del__ for each (the relative order of 'del x' and 'del y' may vary). This is why __del__ alone never guarantees timely teardown for cyclic graphs.

questions.question:
What happens when __del__ itself raises? Run and report both streams:
```python
class A:
    def __del__(self):
        print('inside __del__')
        raise RuntimeError('dying badly')

A()
print('program continues')
```
questions.answer:
stdout:
inside __del__
program continues

stderr:
Exception ignored while calling deallocator <function A.__del__ at 0x...>:
Traceback (most recent call last):
  File "<stdin>", line 4, in __del__
RuntimeError: dying badly

WHY: An exception escaping __del__ can never propagate to user code (nothing can catch code running during deallocation), so CPython prints 'inside __del__' to stdout, swallows the exception, and emits an 'Exception ignored while calling deallocator' notice plus the traceback to stderr. The interpreter does not crash: execution continues with 'program continues'.

questions.question:
Resurrection: __del__ that refuses to let its object die. Predict the output:
```python
class A:
    _graveyard = []
    def __del__(self):
        A._graveyard.append(self)
        print('__del__: instance moved into the graveyard')

a = A()
del a
print('graveyard holds the instance:', len(A._graveyard) == 1)
```
questions.answer:
__del__: instance moved into the graveyard
graveyard holds the instance: True

WHY: When del a drops the reference count to zero, __del__ runs, and appending self to the class-level _graveyard list creates a brand-new reference to the object - this is resurrection. The instance is no longer a cyc-of-fact free object; it lives on inside the graveyard, so the check reports True even though the name a was deleted.

__init__ 2 140243584555312
__init__ 2 140243584555312
True

WHY: Both constructions reuse one cached Small(2) instance from _cache, which is exactly why __init__ fires twice with the SAME id. The cache is a singleton trap: the second constructor call re-initializes the shared object instead of building a new one. int itself cannot be cached by your override (int subclasses still allocate), but your __new__ made it a flyweight.

3 3

WHY: Every successful construction pays one __new__ call and one __init__ call, so three instantiations give 3 + 3. This is the normal 1:1 pairing whenever __new__ returns an instance of the requested class.

object.__new__() takes exactly one argument (the type to instantiate)

WHY: object.__new__ knows nothing about your extra argument x; it performs raw allocation and rejects any additional arguments with TypeError. Even though __new__ itself received x=5 successfully, the explicit call object.__new__(cls, x) passes x along, which object refuses. On CPython the construction dies right there, before __init__ is ever reached.

new, no return
value: None

WHY: Falling off the end of __new__ is an implicit return None, and None is not an A instance, so __init__ is skipped. A() therefore evaluates to None - the same outcome as an explicit return None, no error raised.

questions.question:
Is the object in __init__ the exact object __new__ built? Predict the output:
```python
class A:
    def __new__(cls):
        obj = object.__new__(cls)
        obj.x = 'from new'
        print('in __new__, id =', id(obj))
        return obj
    def __init__(self):
        print('in __init__, id =', id(self), 'x =', self.x)

a = A()
print('same object:', a.x)
```
questions.answer:
in __new__, id = 139791275183040
in __init__, id = 139791275183040 x = from new
same object: from new

WHY: type_call passes the precise return value of __new__ into __init__ as self - no copying. The matching ids prove both hooks manipulated the very same allocation, and the attribute x set during allocation is visible in __init__. Ids are memory addresses and vary per run.

DBCA

WHY: Zero-argument super() uses __class__ plus the instance to walk the MRO of the actual object, which for D is D -> B -> C -> A -> object. Each __init__ prints its letter then delegates to the next class in that single, flattened order, so no class runs twice and 'DBCA' is printed on one line.

questions.question:
Sneaky manual init: calling A.__init__ on an unrelated instance. Predict the output (will it raise?):
```python
class A:
    def __init__(self, v):
        self.v = v

class B:
    pass

b = B()
A.__init__(b, 10)
print(b.v, type(b).__name__)
```
questions.answer:
10 B

WHY: No TypeError. A.__init__ is a plain Python function, so calling it through the class with explicit arguments simply executes the body with b in the self slot - there is no isinstance guard the way built-in descriptors (like object.__init__) enforce. It silently sets b.v = 10 on an unrelated class's instance.

__new__; cls = A
instance type: A

WHY: Invoking A.__new__(A) directly performs only allocation - the type_call machinery that normally fires __init__ is bypassed entirely. obj is a real, albeit uninitialized, instance, which is precisely why the old-school alternative constructor pattern using cls.__new__(cls) leaves the object in an 'empty shell' state.

object.__new__(X): X is not a type object (A)

WHY: object.__new__ expects a class as its sole argument; handing it a live instance confuses the allocator and it refuses with TypeError. The message echoes the type name that was passed. (On CPython 3.13 and earlier the message is worded differently, so rely on the check, not the exact string.)

new
init
TypeError: __init__() should return None, not 'A'

WHY: Even returning the very instance self is a contract violation - the only legal return is None. This is the classic after __new__/after-allocated status check performed by type_call. The allocation and the body of __init__ already ran, so the type name in the error is 'A'.

missing: A.__init__() missing 1 required positional argument: 'b'
extra: A.__init__() takes 3 positional arguments but 4 were given

WHY: A(1) supplies self plus one argument, which is one short, so the call is rejected with a missing-argument message; A(1, 2, 3) overshoots. Both signatures count self internally - the reported numbers already include it ('takes 3' means self, a, b). Since __init__ is a normal method, argument binding errors surface exactly where the method actually is.

new with 5
init with 5
A(5) ok
new with 10
A.__init__() missing 1 required positional argument: 'y'

WHY: Arguments are given to both methods, so A(5) satisfies both signatures. With no arguments, __new__'s default fills x=10 and allocation succeeds (printed), but __init__ has no default for y and rejects the call AFTER allocation. The instance is silently thrown away when the exception propagates.

Derived.__new__
Base False True

WHY: Derived.__new__ returns a bare Base object, which is a superclass - not an instance of cls=Derived. Because it fails the isinstance(cls) check, __init__ is never called. The result is type Base: not a Derived, but still a Base.

Base.__new__ for Derived
Derived.__init__ on Derived

WHY: Base.__new__ inherits and receives cls = Derived, allocating a Derived instance. Initialization, however, is dispatched by the instance's actual type, so Derived.__init__ overrides Base.__init__ and is the one that runs. This shows __new__ resolves by defining class, __init__ by instance type.

questions.question:
Can __init__ overwrite the state planted by __new__? Predict every __dict__ line:
```python
class A:
    def __new__(cls):
        obj = object.__new__(cls)
        obj.secret = 'from __new__'
        print('__new__ sealed:', obj.__dict__)
        return obj
    def __init__(self):
        print('__init__ sees:', self.__dict__)
        self.fresh = ['only in init']
        print('__init__ after:', self.__dict__)

a = A()
print('final:', a.__dict__)
```

questions.answer:
ValueError: invalid literal for int() with base 10: 'not a number'

WHY: Because int defines no initializable __init__, all the actual value parsing must happen inside int.__new__. It tries to decode the string 'not a number' as base-10 digits and fails while still in __new__, so the exception is raised before any __init__ could run. The failure is a ValueError, not a TypeError, because the argument count matched.

5
597

WHY: int.__new__(cls, text, base) parses the string in that base: '101' base 2 is 5, and '255' base 16 is 2*256 + 5*16 + 5 = 597. Even though cls is the subclass, the parse result becomes a MyInt instance. This works because int's own slot __new__ consumes the second argument; object.__new__ would have choked on it.

b'\xc3\xa9' é

WHY: bytes.__new__ accepts the already-encoded raw bytes, so the encoding is done in __new__ via text.encode('utf-8'), turning the single character 'é' into the two-byte sequence b'\xc3\xa9'. b.decode() reverses it. A matching no-op __init__ is needed simply to declare a compatible signature, since bytes is immutable and does the real work in __new__.

TypeError: type 'bool' is not an acceptable base type

WHY: bool is a C-level 'final' type that the interpreter refuses to subclass, so even an empty subclass definition fails immediately at class-creation time, before any __new__ or __init__ exists. No instance is ever created; the TypeError fires while constructing the class itself.

questions.question:
Hidden reference keeps the object alive. Predict the two counted lines:
```python
import gc

class A:
    _cached = None
    dels = 0
    def __new__(cls):
        if cls._cached is None:
            cls._cached = object.__new__(cls)
        return cls._cached
    def __del__(self):
        A.dels += 1
        print('del')

x = A()
del x
gc.collect()
print('dels after del + collect:', A.dels)
del A._cached
gc.collect()
print('dels after cache cleared:', A.dels)
```
questions.answer:
dels after del + collect: 0
del
dels after cache cleared: 1

WHY: Deleting the name x does not free the instance because _cached still references it, and gc.collect() cannot move a reachable object - so __del__ stays dormant and the count reads 0. Only `del A._cached` drops the last reference; __del__ runs immediately (before the next print statement), and the count becomes 1. It is a reminder that a hidden cache reference postpones finalization indefinitely.

questions.question:
Interaction between __del__ and a weakref callback. Predict all three lines:
```python
import weakref, gc

class A:
    def __del__(self):
        print('__del__')

a = A()
reg = weakref.ref(a, lambda r: print('weakref callback'))
del a
gc.collect()
print('collected:', reg() is None)
```
questions.answer:
__del__
weakref callback
collected: True

WHY: When the last strong reference is gone, the object is finalized in two ordered steps: first its __del__ runs, then the weakref callback fires; the callback observes the now-orphaned referent. reg() returns None afterwards because death is complete, so the final check prints True.

goodbye alice

WHY: In this simple non-cyclic case the instance's attributes are still fully intact when __del__ runs - nothing has been reclaimed yet. Accessing self.name works fine and prints 'goodbye alice'. The dangerous cases are cycles or interpreter shutdown, where __del__ may run after parts of the object (or its class/module) have already been torn down.

object.__new__(cls)

WHY: object.__new__(cls) allocates a blank A instance - the standard 'raw make' - and the machinery then calls __init__(self, 1), setting x to 1. Filling the blank with cls(n) instead would call A() recursively from inside __new__, and __new__ would keep calling itself until RecursionError. Only a low-level allocator (object.__new__ or super().__new__) can break the loop.

None

WHY: The type-call machinery demands that __init__ return exactly None; returning any other object (even self) triggers TypeError: __init__() should return None. This example runs without error and prints nothing at all from the try block, because return None satisfies the contract.

RecursionError: maximum recursion depth exceeded

WHY: cls() invokes A.__new__ again from inside A.__new__, which calls cls() yet again - infinite recursive construction with no termination. The correct return is a raw allocation such as object.__new__(cls) or super().__new__(cls); a call expression like cls() is almost never valid inside __new__.

questions.question:
Attribute-carrying int subclass and arithmetic. Predict each printed line:
```python
class MyInt(int):
    def __new__(cls, n):
        obj = int.__new__(cls, n)
        obj.origin = 'custom'
        return obj
    def __init__(self, n):
        print('init', n)

a = MyInt(3)
b = MyInt(5)
print(a, b, a + b, type(a + b).__name__)
```
questions.answer:
init 3
init 5
3 5 8 int

WHY: __new__ attaches the instance attribute 'origin' (working because a Python int subclass has a dict by default) and __init__ still runs per instance. Arithmetic dispatches to int's slot implementation, which produces a plain int rather than a MyInt, so a + b is 8 with type int and the custom attribute is not carried over.

questions.question:
Interleaved construction traces. Give the complete output:
```python
class A:
    count = 0
    def __new__(cls):
        obj = object.__new__(cls)
        A.count += 1
        obj.serial = A.count
        print('new serial', obj.serial)
        return obj
    def __init__(self):
        print('init serial', self.serial)

a = A()
b = A()
c = A()
print(a.serial, b.serial, c.serial)
```
questions.answer:
new serial 1
init serial 1
new serial 2
init serial 2
new serial 3
init serial 3
1 2 3

WHY: Each construction pairs a __new__ call (which stamps serial from the class counter) immediately followed by its __init__. The traces interleave strictly per-instruction: new 1, init 1, new 2, init 2, new 3, init 3 - proving __new__ and __init__ interleave across separate calls the way a single expression would. Each instance keeps its own serial, and the final line prints 1 2 3.

questions.question:
Predict the output:

class A:
    def __del__(self):
        print('del A')

x = A()
del x
print('done')
questions.answer:
del A
done

When del x is executed, the reference count of the object drops to zero immediately, so Python calls __del__ synchronously before continuing. This is reference-count destruction — no garbage collector involved.

in f
del B 2
del B 1
after

Local variables in a frame are destroyed in reverse creation order (LIFO) when the frame is destroyed on return. B(2) is created last so y is destroyed first, triggering its __del__ before x's.

questions.question:
Predict the output:

class C:
    def __del__(self):
        print('del C')

x = C()
y = x
del x
print('after del x')
del y
print('end')
questions.answer:
after del x
del C
end

del x removes one reference but y still holds a reference to the same object, so the refcount is still 1 and __del__ is not called. Only when del y drops the refcount to zero does __del__ fire.

questions.question:
Predict the output:

import gc

class D:
    def __del__(self):
        print('del D')

a = D()
a.ref = a
del a
print('before gc')
gc.collect()
print('after gc')
questions.answer:
before gc
del D
after gc

Self-referencing a.ref = a means del a does NOT drop the refcount to zero (refcount stays 1 from the cycle). The cycle garbage collector must collect the cycle, and only then does __del__ run.

questions.question:
Predict the output:

import gc

class D:
    def __del__(self):
        print('del D')

a = D()
b = D()
a.ref = b
b.ref = a
del a, b
print('before gc')
gc.collect()
print('done')
questions.answer:
before gc
del D
del D
done

Both objects form a mutual cycle. del a and del b drop the external refcounts to 1 (from the cycle links), so neither __del__ runs immediately. gc.collect() detects the unreachable cycle and calls __del__ on both.

init start
caught
del F
end

__new__ creates the instance successfully, but __init__ raises. Since x is never assigned (the exception propagates before assignment), the partially-constructed object's refcount drops to zero and __del__ fires immediately.

questions.question:
Predict the output (a traceback also goes to stderr):

class E:
    def __del__(self):
        print('del E start')
        raise RuntimeError('boom')

x = E()
del x
print('end')
questions.answer:
del E start
end
(On stderr: 'Exception ignored while calling deallocator ... RuntimeError: boom')

An exception raised inside __del__ is swallowed by CPython with a warning to stderr. It does not propagate. The program continues normally — 'end' prints after 'del E start'.

questions.question:
Predict the output (order of 'del A' vs 'weakref cb' matters):

import weakref

class A:
    def __del__(self):
        print('del A')

def cb(ref):
    print('weakref cb')

a = A()
wr = weakref.ref(a, cb)
del a
print('done')
questions.answer:
del A
weakref cb
done

When an object is destroyed by reference counting (refcount hits zero directly), CPython calls __del__ first, then fires the weakref callback. This is the opposite of the cycle-GC collection order shown in the next question.

questions.question:
Predict the output (order matters — PEP 442 semantics):

import gc, weakref

class B:
    def __del__(self):
        print('del B')

def cb(ref):
    print('weakref cb')

b = B()
b.ref = b  # cycle
wr = weakref.ref(b, cb)
del b
gc.collect()
print('done')
questions.answer:
weakref cb
del B
done

When the garbage collector collects a cycle, weakref callbacks fire BEFORE the finalizer __del__ (PEP 442). This is the reverse of the refcount-destruction order in the previous question. PEP 442 runs callbacks first so a finalizer cannot resurrect an object that callbacks still reference.

questions.question:
Predict the output:

import gc

holder = []

class A:
    def __del__(self):
        print('del A called')
        holder.append(self)

a = A()
